newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stocks may slide, Deng death mostly discounted.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks may slide, Deng death mostly discounted.

text.p: The Hong Kong stock market could mark the passing of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping with a symbolic, kneejerk fall on Thursday, but analysts said his death has long been discounted.

"Probably to a large extent it has been discounted because of the rumours of the past week but I think that generally a kneejerk reaction is expected with perhaps the market dropping three or four hundred points," said Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage.
"But many people might also regard this as a buying opportunity too and so the market may be quite volatile," he said.
Concerns about Deng Xiaoping's health contributed to a recent slide in Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index.
From an all-time high of 14,004.93 on January 16, the blue-chip barometer has tumbled 899 points to Wednesday's close of 13,106.32.
"This is something that stock markets have been gearing up for for some considerable time," said Peter Churchouse, regional strategist at Morgan Stanley.

"People have got used to the idea and thought long and hard about likely directions in China post-Deng anyway. People have got their own views and have become more or less comfortable with them," he said.
Analysts said investors' attention would be focused on the reaction within China itself on Thursday.
"For the first time ever foreign markets will look to Shenzhen and Shanghai reactions as a benchmark rather than the other way round," said Churchouse.
Many analysts say the transition of power in China seemed to be a done deal with Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin having already consolidated his position as Deng's successor.
But investors would be watching for signs of a power struggle in Beijing and any possible changes to China's stance towards the outside world - in particular Hong Kong and Taiwan.

"Many people are not concerned about the succession because they think it is all in place. There are others who will say that now the lid comes off Pandora's Box and it could be a bit rocky in Beijing for a while. This is the more pessimistic view," Gorges said.
Investors have also been anticipating a smooth transition to Chinese rule for Hong Kong, an issue which has helped drive Hong Kong stocks to record levels over recent months.
"The financial community particularly is optimistic," Gorges said.
Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
Investors would also be looking for any changes in economic policy, since Deng was the creator of sweeping economic reforms in China after taking power in 1979.
"Deng has been a fast-track reformer," Churchouse said.

"There is a body of opinion there which suggests that it should slow down and that the nature and pace of reform brings into question the extent to which state-owned enterprises will be let go to the wall in the interests of reform," he said.
But analysts said the recent unease which has been plaguing Hong Kong stock prices would now be removed.

"That is why quite a lot of people would buy on weakness. There have been rumours for years on the subject so it does get it out of the way but on the otherhand you cannot deny that it does create some uncertainty as well," Gorges said.
